utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mustac. If I could remind you that you are under affirmation to tell the truth. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mustac.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me when you joined the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of November, 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And when was the party established?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established in the same year, on the 17th of June, if memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that you were a member right from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your name was put forward by the party for the parliamentary elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were then elected member of parliament on behalf of the HDZ in the same year?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ, won a landslide victory in 1990 and took over power in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: How many members of parliament were there who came originally from Dubrovnik in the first Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four of us all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many of the four of you were members of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: What was your official position in the HDZ of the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the vice-president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The HDZ, was it also in power at the local level in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You, as a deputy to the Croatian parliament, did you speak on behalf of the citizens of Dubrovnik while you were a deputy to the parliament?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to protect their interests as best as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you protect the interests of the town of Dubrovnik as best as you could also in the period under discussion, in the second half of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: While working as an MP, did you follow all the important developments in the town of Dubrovnik that could have been of significance for your work as an MP?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my best to follow everything that was going on that was important for my own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to your position at the Sponza Palace in the months of September, October, November, and December 1991, did you have any other official position in the town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the head of the state archives and a member of the Croatian parliament. I did not hold any other posts in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you then agree with me that at the time you had a widespread network of contacts with important people in the town of Dubrovnik, people in important positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since I was an MP, I had a lot to do with people in important positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it important for your work, as an MP, that you were well informed on all developments in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, that was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you work in order to obtain information so that you could tell the other MPs in the Croatian parliament and at the republican level exactly what was going on in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I did my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you leave Dubrovnik between October and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember when specifically the first time was, and the second?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first was on the 8th of October, and the next time was between the 1st and the 2nd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly yesterday when you said that the second time you left Dubrovnik had to do with a parliament session at which the independence of the Republic of Croatia was declared?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did I understand you correctly that when you left Dubrovnik on that occasion, before you left, you had talked to Mr. Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your conversation with Marinovic preceded the session of the parliament at which Croatia declared its independence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same day, just before I travelled, I talked to General, then Colonel, Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you then agree with me that this conversation of yours with Colonel Marinovic was not in November but rather in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My departure took place between the 1st and the 2nd of November, and the conversation took place just before I had set out. Before I left, I talked to Colonel Marinovic. It was on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will it be of any assistance to you if I tell you that the session of parliament you're talking about was not held on the 8th of November but on the 8th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of November, or on the 8th of November, that's when Croatia's independence was declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How often were you in touch with people from Dubrovnik's Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not regular contacts, but very sporadic and quite accidental, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you did tell us yesterday, didn't you, that the Crisis Staff dealt with all the important issues, issues that affected the life of Dubrovnik's citizens?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Whenever there was something I had to know, I would go to them to ask questions about supply, about water supply, if they were facing any problems, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other source of information of what was going on in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were official conversations, but I did have unofficial contact with other citizens too, where I got information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you, and how often, if so, contact with the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were frequent contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How often were you in touch with the commander of the town's defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less often, because I was in the Old Town, and they were outside the Old Town. I'm talking about the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there, at the time, two main concerns for every citizen of Dubrovnik: Firstly, the defence of Dubrovnik, and secondly, the supplies? Was there anything that prevented you at the time from establishing frequent contact with the commander of the defence and the Crisis Staff, or perhaps my reading of events at the time is not quite correct.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had more frequent contacts with the Crisis Staff, and I had very little contact with the command of the town's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you weren't interested in how the defence was proceeding?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was simply not my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in the town's defence, there were no problems to be conveyed to the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there were. As I said before, I talked to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know about that. But what I'm asking you is how you can explain this little, rather little interest that you had in these problems.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I didn't say that there was only little interest on my part. I said that I did not have many opportunities to talk to key people in the town's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew Mr. Nojko Marinovic rather well.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known him since the time he left his position as commander back at Trebinje and arrived in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You had not known him prior to that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in negotiations regarding his transfer from Trebinje to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who did?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the mayor of Dubrovnik was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once when we talked, he told me that he had had a talk with Colonel Marinovic, following which Colonel Marinovic arrived in Dubrovnik. I don't know specifically where and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he also tell you what he had promised Colonel Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you what Colonel Marinovic had asked of him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many times, roughly speaking, did you see Nojko Marinovic between the time he arrived in Dubrovnik and the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About four times, three or four times. Four, I think, is on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in his office, which at the time was at the Zagreb Hotel in Lapad. I also saw him once when I was strolling about town. We had a brief conversation. And twice, again in the town itself. One of these times was just before I left Dubrovnik to attend the parliament session in Zagreb. That's as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see him strolling about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the Old Town also.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see him on the last two occasions you saw him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I saw him was between the 1st and the 2nd of November, before I left Dubrovnik to attend the parliament session I talked about in Zagreb. I never saw him again after that. He had been wounded and we never met again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you concerned about the town's defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did care a great deal about what was going on in that respect, but those were not my competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you about. Were you concerned?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to get as much information as possible on how things were going regarding the defence of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which specific units of the National Guard Corps were stationed in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what the names of those units were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many units there were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you travelled to Zagreb to inform the Croatian parliament on the developments, was there no need for you to obtain exact information as to how many soldiers there were, what sort of weapons they had, what their needs were, where exactly they were positioned? Weren't those crucial questions at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, by all means they were. I knew all of that. I knew that they had a very small amount of weapons, not very powerful weapons, to boot. I don't know exactly how many there were. I think it would be ridiculous for me to venture a guess when I don't really know how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a very bald figure.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I'd say about 30, but that's only my impression. Perhaps there were more, perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps think to ask Mr. Marinovic about the exact number of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him what sort of weapons he needed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him; rather, he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was it he told you? What sort of weapons was he after?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before I left, by boat, for Rijeka, as I said, this was between the 1st and the 2nd --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, just to keep things brief: What sort of weapons did he say he needed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, quite literally: "Please, tell General Tus on my behalf that the town of Dubrovnik lacks all weapons and ammunition. We only have one recoilless gun, very little ammunition, and it's impossible for us to defend ourselves with what we have. Please tell him that we need urgent help in terms of weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long was this conversation between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an extremely brief conversation. I was just about to board the ship. Three minutes, four minutes, certainly less than five.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Marinovic asked you to go to Zagreb and to ask for weapons to defend the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me specifically to convey his message about the lack of weapons to General Tus.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Colonel Marinovic did not have direct contact with the headquarters in Zagreb, the army headquarters?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that specifically. He must have had some sort of contact. What sort of contact exactly, I didn't know, but he must have had good reason to tell me, because I was a member of parliament, and there must have been a reason for him to tell me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he perhaps tell you, once given weapons, how he was going to bring these weapons into town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he told me nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So he was asking for weapons. Does that probably mean he believed there was a way to bring these weapons into town, otherwise he wouldn't have been asking for weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds logical, but I have no idea how exactly he was going to bring weapons into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me if I say that since he was asking for weapons, he probably assumed that he could bring weapons into town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably his view, his take on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Croatian army was positioned around the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I do know that some of them were at the Zagreb Hotel, but where exactly they were positioned, I don't know and I never thought to ask. It's a very small town. Whether it's a hundred metres in this or that direction. It's really immaterial, and I'm not even sure those positions changed over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar specifically with any single position of the Croatian army within the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some troops were stationed at Lapad, but as for the rest, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you see at Lapad?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. I merely said that I knew about their headquarters having been established there. I said that I met Mr. Marinovic there once, and that's all I can tell you about their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which route did you take when you went from the Old Town, where you stayed, to Lapad? Which streets specifically?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the street that takes you there, Iva Vojnovica Street. You take a left turn at one point, that's the Lapad promenade, which is a road that takes you straight to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you leave the Old Town, which gate do you take?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to Lapad, I took the Pile gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what's the next street after the Pile gate when you head for Lapad?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it bears a different name, I believe, than it did at the time. Then there's a traffic light. You take a left turn and that's Iva Vojnovica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What's the name of this street that was called differently at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think now it's Starcevica Street, but believe me, I can't be sure. We just go there, but we never think about the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this the street leading from the Pile gate to the old hospital at Boninovo?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you take that street -- past the traffic light?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, past the traffic light to the left, that's Vojnovica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But that's not what I'm asking. Between the old hospital at Boninovo and the Pile gate, to the left is the Gradac park; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see what was there in the park?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you look at all -- were you looking while you were walking? You did go on foot, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you never looked left or right on your way there, having taken Starcevica Street past the hospital at Boninovo?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did look both left and right, but if you've ever past there yourself, the same road, you know that there are rows and houses both sides and that all you can see are walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many long-barrel weapons were stationed in Dubrovnik at the time? When I say "long-barrel weapons," I mean all kinds of weapons that aren't just pistols. How many, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about this. I only know what I was told by Colonel Marinovic, and I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many? A rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't venture a guess there. It would be pointless for me to talk about a rough estimate, when it would be totally unfounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's say that there were about 30 defenders in town, and I assume that the number of long barrels was about the same.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that already in March 1991, the police station in Dubrovnik, there were over 500 pieces of long barrels, according to the report of that police station itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re -- could you pause, please, Mr. -- Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to this evidence. It's irrelevant, and it's purely speculative. The witness has clearly answered a number of times he just does not know anything about the defences of Dubrovnik. And my learned friend keeps putting things to him, and the witness keeps saying: "I don't know." It's just wasting the Tribunal's time, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. You can put the question you're in the process of putting, Mr. Petrovic, but you are just persistently putting matters that the witness does say he knows no answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you'll allow me to reply. This is a person that we're talking about who is a deputy to the parliament, who is familiar with all the details of the goings-on in the city of Dubrovnik, who is going to Zagreb to seek weapons for Dubrovnik and who knows nothing about it. This is not an ordinary citizen of Dubrovnik that we're talking about. This is a person who, in the line of his duty, had to be familiar in detail with the situation of the defence of the city of Dubrovnik, whereas he is denying any such knowledge. And this is why I'm pursuing this particular line of questioning and asking this particular question. If you find it superfluous, I shall refrain from any such questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's why I indicated to you, Mr. Petrovic, that you may put the question that you had been asking. I appreciate fully what you're doing, but I also point out, as Mr. Re has pointed out, that there's little point in you continuing to put questions to be told the witness knows no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what is your reply to my last question?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The question whether you knew that already in March 1991, 534 pieces of long-barrels were in the possession of the police station in the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret the fact that you believe that I do not wish to answer. I do wish to tell you what I do know. This is -- this police never reported to me what the number of weapons in their possession was, nor was it my duty to ask them about it. Probably they had the number of weapons that you say that they said they had. I'm not denying that they had it, but I never asked them, nor did they ask me. That is the problem. So please do not say that I do not wish to reply. I have taken a solemn oath before this Court to the effect that I will be saying the truth, and I have said the truth, and the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and that is in the interests of my own people and all the other peoples on this planet, for the truth to be told here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see soldiers of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many of them did you see?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city of Dubrovnik was a centre where people came. They came to have a coffee, to have an ice-cream cone. How many did I see? Now you're asking me some 12 years later, after the fact, about particular numbers. People moved about. They were not prisoners. They moved about freely. But I did not see armed soldiers in the town of Dubrovnik. That is the question. I saw policemen, yes, I did, but not soldiers. I saw soldiers, but not with arms, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give a statement to the investigators of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the month of September nineteen-ninety --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. The interpreter is lost about the year because of the overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you give this statement to be Mr. Arshad?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you say on that occasion everything that you knew and everything which was the truth?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the statement read out to you before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did it reflect what you said about the events that you were asked about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see in the Old Town of Dubrovnik any armed soldiers of the Croatian army when they came to have this ice cream or have some coffee?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see soldiers with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then: Why did you say to investigator Arshad the following: "Several times I saw people in civilian clothes with weapons walking about the old city? I believe I'm sure that they came to see their relatives and their friends"? Why did you say this to Mr. Arshad if you had never seen any soldiers with arms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's exactly what I said. What I did say was that I had seen soldiers. They were not in uniform. You can say that those were uniforms that they were wearing. I'll allow the possibility I may have said this. I may have expressed myself in this way. And I may have seen them. I may have seen some of them. But these were people from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So let us note: You saw soldiers with weapons in the old city. Whatever they were wearing, you saw them.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could put it that way. I saw some. Well, we can say something to that effect. Now, what weapons, what exactly was perhaps a pistol or something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects. The witness didn't say soldiers he said civilians. My learned friend is going to put an extract from the witness's statement to him. In fairness to the witness, and so the Tribunal knows what the witness said in his statement, if he's trying to say that he -- impeach him with a prior inconsistent statement, he should read the extract in its entirety to the witness and ask him if he said it and stands by it. It's the proper way of doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I read exactly -- you can see here in the transcript what I read: "Several times I saw people in civilian clothes with weapons strolling about the old city." This is what I read, and I hope this is the way it has been translated for you. So I did not quote mistakenly what has been put down in the statement. Tell me, colleague, what was it that I omitted to read or read wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the English version I have in my hand said: "On two occasions, I encountered with armed men in the Old Town, once on the Pile gate and the second time on the Ploca gate. On both occasions they were civilian patrols. However, I did see a couple of times some people in plain clothes, carrying rifles, roaming around in the Old Town." The next sentence says: "But I am sure that they came to see their relatives or friends and had no military designs in the Old Town." Now, that proposition is quite different to the one my learned friend is putting to the witness, that is, that they were soldiers. In fairness, he should put the entire paragraph to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber, of course, is at the disadvantage that it has neither version, so it cannot know fully what you are saying. But, Mr. Petrovic, if the B/C/S version is similar to that which has just been read by Mr. Re, what you have been putting to the witness is quite incomplete and is misleading when you just pull out one sentence from it. So that it may be useful if you put to him the full passage and then ask him your questions again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I will do so hereafter. In fact, I was given from the witness a reply which confirms what I said, the respect of whether I read the paragraph in extents [as interpreted] or not. The witness said that he had seen armed people who were soldiers in the old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did these people that you saw in the old city have?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that these were ridiculous weapons, as weapons go. These are some trophy rifles. Well, I'm not very versed in the weapons field, but it was something quite outdated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did any of them have automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the weapon -- what kind of weapons did you see?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was a soldier. I had been a soldier myself. So these were rifles that were very old, ancient. I cannot really describe them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But how, then, do you know that these are not modern rifles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know what modern rifles look like. I'm quite capable, I'm quite mature, and I'm quite capable to distinguish between rifles and between other things, between sophisticated and outdated things generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see these modern rifles in Dubrovnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I see them. I don't know. I simply don't know. Maybe I did, maybe I did not. I don't know why you're asking me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please try harder. Yesterday you were quite sure about details and days that had taken place 13 days [as interpreted] ago. Just tell me: Did you see people with modern weapons in the city of Dubrovnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the city of Dubrovnik at the time, I did not see any such persons with such modern weapons, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? I saw them both outside the city -- perhaps you're asking me about things, wanting me to tell you that I saw things that I don't know at this time when I saw these things, because I'm not quite sure about these weapons. You're asking about automatic weapons, and I can tell you, as I say, that I haven't seen any such weapons in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any such weapons outside the centre of the town? I'm not asking when; just did you see.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any policemen in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how were these policemen armed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policemen had pistols. They were armed with pistols. They had their batons. They -- whether they had any other arms, I cannot recall at this point, although I do allow for the possibility that they could have had some, but I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you allow that they could have had?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual weapons that a policeman carries, and that is, of course, up to the particular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the police perhaps have automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any, but I'm not denying that they might have had them, but I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How were the Dubrovnik defence units organised before Nojko Marinovic arrived in town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were amateurish, amateur units, as it were, which had been set up according to the -- on a voluntary basis, on a voluntary criteria, and for the most part poorly organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When were these amateur units established?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they existed at the end of September, certainly. They were in existence then, at the end of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did Nojko Marinovic arrive in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nojko Marinovic arrived in 1991, around September also, I believe. But I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So were these units in existence prior to his arrival?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since when was it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I know that the National Guard Corps had been established at the end of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I fail to understand this. Nojko Marinovic came in September, these units were formed in September. When was this situation of disarray, poor organisation, and amateur units, when was this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came, Nojko Marinovic did not assume this command. What I said was that I knew that at the end of September, there existed the National Guard Corps. I did not say that it was established then. I said that I knew that at that time they were in existence already. They may have been formed before, but in the month of September --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the month of September, inform the parliament about the situation of the National Guard Corps units in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my duty to inform, as you put it, in detail. My reports were of a general character, about the situation in the town itself. You are asking me now about the beginning, and I've told you I don't know when the National Guard Corps was set up in Dubrovnik. But I did say that it was in September. As far as I can recall -- that is as far as I can recall. But it could have been earlier, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you tell the parliament about the National Guard Corps in September?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to the parliament in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Prior to September, did you submit any reports or talk to anyone about the situation concerning the National Guard Corps and the town's defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to make this clear: The town's defence was not my job, was not my concern. It was the concern of the mayor and his people. Those were his contacts. The organisation was up to him. That was part of his job. My duty was when I spoke in the parliament, to briefly review those matters too, but that was not the only thing I was supposed to talk about. We had great responsibilities and great duties. This was not the only thing, because the situation in Croatia back at the time was like that. Whenever the parliament met, it didn't meet to deal with these matters only.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So help me out with this, please. As a member of parliament, from the party in power, at the time of all these developments that you told us about yesterday, did you sort of refer to it in passing during the sessions of the parliament, only in passing? What, then, was the main subject of your discussion? What was the key issue for you, in view of everything that was happening in Dubrovnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were not my words. That was your understanding of what I said. When I spoke, I closely followed the agenda of the meeting. It was about the various laws that were being passed at the time. There was little opportunity to speak about what was happening in Dubrovnik. You had, for example, the item usually referred to as miscellaneous. It should be easy to verify what the specific agenda was on any of the dates that parliament met. It should be equally easy to verify what individual MPs were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did the situation in Dubrovnik change after Nojko Marinovic's arrival?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It changed a great deal. He was a professional soldier. He knew his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did he do to improve the town's defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was more safety. People felt safer and felt that they were being looked after by someone. Up to that point, it had been a bit laughable, as I said, and I stand by that characterisation. Now the whole thing took on an entirely different character, and everyone trusted the man who was in charge. Everyone trusted that he would do the best for the town's defence and that he would not allow the town to fall into the enemy's hands, that he would stand up and defend the town. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So Nojko Marinovic came along and organised those 30 defenders in such a way as to prevent the town from being taken by the JNA; is that a correct rendering of what you said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that's a mischaracterisation. You keep referring to a specific figure. I said right at the beginning when you asked me how many people there were in the National Guard Corps. I said I don't know. If I say 30, that's just a very bald figure I'm giving you there. It could be more, it could be less. That's what I said when you asked me. Upon Colonel Marinovic's arrival, the whole thing changed. Now, how many troops there were then, the National Guard Corps or whatever they call themselves, certainly more. As for the specific figure, I never asked him, nor was it my responsibility to ask him, nor did it seem becoming to inquire about that. I trusted him fully and believed that he knew what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How was this change felt among the people of Dubrovnik, this change? How did it affect life in Dubrovnik, Nojko Marinovic coming over, bringing with him his reputation of a good professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were much happier about things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was it that suddenly made you happier?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep repeating the same thing ad nauseam. I wonder where we are getting at. As I said, up to that point it had all been rather laughable. Those were just petty amateurs. Suddenly, there was a man who knew what he was doing, and we all trusted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But specifically, what did it look like after his arrival? What changed? I want a specific change, an example of a specific change, something that you observed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Prior to Nojko Marinovic's arrival, the defence was organised in an amateurish and laughable way?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After his arrival, things began to change. What exactly was this change reflected in after his arrival?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a man who knew his job. He organised the town's defence the way he thought it best, and we trusted him. I'm not familiar with any details regarding this, nor did I ask questions. Contact between Colonel Nojko Marinovic and the town's defence was the responsibility of the mayor. It wasn't my duty or my responsibility, nor did I have any detailed knowledge of what exactly went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Throughout those months we're talking about, did you ever see the Croatian army fire from inside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any activities by the Croatian army from within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, with the exception of the 6th of December. That's when I heard. But I did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you hear on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that -- I mean when I say, "I heard," it was common knowledge. Everyone knew that a decisive clash was being fought out at the Imperijal fort. I can't say that it was a proper battle, because the odds were not even. And on the part of the town's defence, there was a mortar that was being used by the town's defence, one or several, in the direction of the Imperijal fortress, and the attackers who were attacking the fort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear where this mortar was positioned and where it was firing from?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I know that the general location was at Lapad. You keep telling me it was at Gradac. Now, whether it was Gradac specifically, I really can't say. I can't, however, rule out the possibility that there was something at Gradac also; it's just that I didn't know. I had no personal knowledge of this. You must keep in mind one thing that I said yesterday. I was commuting between Dubrovnik, Zagreb, and Rijeka this whole time. On the 27th I arrived in the hospital. I had taken ill with salmonella. I left hospital on the 4th of December still feeling very ill, and it was hardly possible for me to monitor movements by the Croatian units. Because you seem to expect me to come up with specific bits of information, whereas I really can't. I'm only telling you what I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we can say with certainty that before the 6th of December, you never heard any mortars firing, any rifles firing from within the Old Town on the JNA positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That will be sufficient. Thank you. Is the name Milivoj Minica [phoen] familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Djuro Korda is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Djuro Korda was the chief of police at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet him in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several times. We are from the same town. We are acquaintances. We've known each other even before 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: He was -- you were an MP. You were a citizen of Dubrovnik, and you had known the man for a long time. Did you ever talk to him and ask him what the needs of the town's defence were, what they needed in order to defend the town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have asked him, it's just that I can't remember specifically what I asked him or whether I asked him anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss the developments in Dubrovnik and around Dubrovnik at all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not discuss that. I didn't talk to him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you're certain that you didn't talk about that, then what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know how it is when old acquaintances meet: How have you been? How's life's been treating you? Just exchanging pleasantries. I didn't address him as the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You are an MP, the town is under siege. Your town is under siege. You meet the chief of police and your only exchange -- you only exchanged pleasantries. Am I correct in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. It was only very rarely in those difficult times, in that time of crisis that I came across him, because that's how the situation was. He spent most of his time outside the town walls, because the police headquarters were at Lapad, what we called the Lapad police station, near the water polo club. And I was stationed within the Old Town walls. Therefore, there wasn't much communication between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you know his location? How did you know that he was outside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dubrovnik is where I come from. Of course, everyone knows where the police station is. I'm not sure if you're familiar with its whereabouts, but I am very well aware of the respective locations of the police station, the kindergarten, the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the police station as such. I asked you about a specific person, and you said you knew where that person was based. How did you know where this person was based? I'm not talking about the police station.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's simple. He was the chief of police. I was the chief archivist and he was the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Colonel Katanic was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what about Captain Cengija?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that person. I know the person. I never met the person but I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was also a police officer. That's what he did. That was his job. But I never personally talked to him; not then, not later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything you heard about that man?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he was with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Aziz Suljevic is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's another police officer. I met this man. I didn't exactly talk to him. We did perhaps say hello. But I know that he was in active service when the ships were coming and going, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about him in the months of October, November, and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the SDK building at the Pile gate is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was there inside the building at the period of time we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the INA oil company building is in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was in that building at the relevant period of time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the SDK building and the INA building, where are these two buildings in relation to the Old Town centre?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDK building is between the Pile gate and the old hospital, to the left of the road. And the INA oil company building, they had several buildings in Dubrovnik. I'm not sure which one you mean. There are several buildings that are at least related to the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the INA building in Dubrovnik," that sounds ambiguous to you. You don't know where that building happens to be?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite what I'm saying, but the oil company, the INA, I believe their headquarters were at the Lapad station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik, people usually refer to that as the INA building, the headquarters; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I'm not trying to lead you a merry dance there. I'm not trying to hide anything from you. To be quite honest, at this moment, I believe that the INA building -- well, yes. I think that's near the court building, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is that in relation to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You leave the Old Town. There's a crossroads to the left, there's Vojnovica Street, and if you go straight, that's Starcevica Street, and you soon reach the INA headquarters. You walk past the national health centre and then that should be the second or third building to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In terms of specific distance in metres, for example, what do you think the distance would be?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the second or third bus stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you reach General Tus?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a request for information in the parliament. I was told where he was based at the time, and he was based at Dubravkin Put. Once I arrived, they told me that the headquarters were shelled where General Tus was stationed, that it had been hit by a rocket, by a missile, and that General Tus had moved headquarters. But I wasn't told specifically where they had gone to. I remained adamant, but they refused to tell me. I went back to them. I told them -- I made clear that I needed to speak to him, and then they said that it was somewhere on Tkalciceva Street in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell General Tus that you would be coming to see him to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My visit was not announced, because they had no idea where he was. His headquarters had just been hit by a missile.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was his official position at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the HQ of what was then referred to as the National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The period of time you're talking about now, were there any organised units of the Croatian army led by Antun Tus or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such organised units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a law governing the establishment and structure of the Croatian army at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say specifically off the top of my head right now. I must have known at the time, but right now I can't remember whether there was in fact a specific law governing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you went to the headquarters of the National Guard Corps. You knocked on a door and you were received by the chief. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I asked whether I could see him. I inquired, and at his former headquarters, which he had since abandoned, they told me he was no longer around. I needed to ask several times before I was told that he was now based in Tkalciceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they want to know why you were looking for him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They asked no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you say who you were?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you also say why you wanted to see him?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't tell those soldiers that I spoke to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who attended the meeting you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tus and myself. Only the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long was the meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very short. I'm telling you, and please do your best to believe me, I walked up and down Tkalciceva Street, and at one point I saw a tall man who approached me. I told the driver to pull over. I'd only seen photographs of this before, but I'd never met him in person. So I approached this tall man and asked him whether he was General Tus. He smiled and he said: "Yes, I am." And he ushered me into the house in Tkalciceva Street. It was just a plain room with a map on the wall, a table, and a set of chairs. We sat down. I told him what I had been told myself by Colonel Marinovic. He placed a hand on my shoulder and told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: There's no need to go into that now. You've already told us about this. So General Tus was just casually strolling about town, you were driving by, you saw him from inside the car, you approached him, and he took you to his office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, that's not a correct reading. But I could tell you something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You shouldn't be saying things like this, he was casually strolling about town. His location was secret at the time. No one knew where he was based. Because his headquarters had just been shelled. I was going up and down Tkalciceva Street just been accident, because I had been given his rough location. And I saw a man wearing a uniform outside a house, so I approached him, and that's how we met. You keep saying "strolling about casually." What is that supposed to mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, in addition to this one sentence, is it your submission to us that there was nothing else you told him about the town's defence, about the situation in Dubrovnik, if the JNA was attacking, where and when, what the forces being deployed were, or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did tell him that the town was in grave danger. I conveyed Colonel Marinovic's words to him exactly. And my final question was: What were the prospects that we were facing? What can we do without weapons? And he said: I really don't know. And he looked very concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he seem surprised when he heard what you said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He seemed greatly concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you find it possible to believe that he didn't know what was going on in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he did know. He must have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you say anything specific to him about the specific defence problems, apart from the general fact that there were no arms?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in charge of the defence. I really didn't know. The only thing -- what I knew, I knew from what Colonel Marinovic had told me, and that was official information that the city was faced with a grave danger because it had nothing to defend itself with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You referred to a recoilless gun. What is it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what Colonel Marinovic told me. He said: "Tell them that we have a -- one recoilless gun in a state of proper repair." Don't ask me. I have no way to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From this time distance, do you know that Colonel Marinovic told you the truth, or perhaps not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to this. My learned friend has asked a series of purely speculative questions of this witness over the course of the last 45 minutes. The difficulty with trying to object at the time is the answer is given and a new question is being asked which is why we haven't objected before, but we do ask Your Honours to please ask my learned friend not to ask these sorts of speculative questions. The witness can't possibly answer these.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I hope you take heed of the point being made as well, Mr. Petrovic. Thank you. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any initiatives from the city of Dubrovnik itself to deal with the existing problems?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city of Dubrovnik had its mayor, with his associates, representatives of the Executive Council and other councils; and on the other hand, we had Colonel Marinovic with the defence structure. I was a deputy, and my predominant duty - I want everybody to know - was official work in the parliament, according to the agenda determined for each particular session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you at every parliamentary session have the situation in the Republic of Croatia on the agenda, as an item on the agenda, because of the aggression, as they put it at that time, from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did the majority of sessions have this item on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't, because this could be placed on the agenda only under the miscellaneous, other business agenda, and we had to follow the agenda, as it was fixed in advance. You cannot change it during the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you submitting that in the autumn of 1991, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia talked about the situation in the Republic of Croatia under the other business item?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not what I'm saying. But I did say it was not the first item on our agenda of our sessions. I said it was discussed, but not at every session as the major item.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the -- in the fall of 1991, during the Vukovar and Dubrovnik events, what was the main theme on the agenda of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The items of the agenda follow the agenda as established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any initiative from the city of Dubrovnik to deal with the problems that existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were any negotiations being conducted at the time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the city of Dubrovnik, there existed a standing commission for relations with the Yugoslav army, or a group of people, or a commission, we can call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who were the people in this commission?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of this commission were Mr. Niksa Obuljen, Mr. Kolic, Mr. Macan, and perhaps some other persons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about their work?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask them if I came across them, but in December, in November, I simply did not have sufficient time to establish -- to -- for any such contacts with them, because I already had a busy schedule, as I have already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you, as a representative of the town of Dubrovnik, of the citizens of Dubrovnik in the Croatian parliament, at all show an interest in the negotiations being conducted between the JNA and the authorities, except for these accidental meetings?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I was very concerned and interested in these, but I did not inform parliament about these because they got first-hand information about the negotiations being conducted from the head of the commission, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you only happened to find out about what was going on in a chance meeting too, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. If I could, if I did have the opportunity, I would certainly have shown an interest in what was going on and the actual state of the negotiations, but my concern, my interest, could in no way influence their actual course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it could have influenced the course, but it was -- what I'm asking is whether you were bent on having precise information about it or not.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have information. I knew that they went to Cavtat for negotiations on several occasions. I also knew that they had been told some things which they had conveyed to me, things that have not been respected by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the content of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the [indiscernible]. At the end of it all, the bottom line was to cease bombing and stop the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did they negotiate with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the actual names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear about -- do you at all know what the supreme state council of the Republic of Croatia is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this was a party which existed in the beginning. Now, whether it was in 1991, well, I cannot say anything on that subject competently. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this is a body which was composed of the highest officials of the Republic of Croatia, headed by the president of the republic, the Prime Minister, the key ministers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll allow that possibility, yes. It could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I cannot speak competently on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the Supreme Defence Council ever addressed by the assembly of the municipality of Dubrovnik, the Executive Council, or other authorities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say that they didn't. I simply don't know. But by the nature of things, I'll allow that it really could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that on the 11th of November, 1991, these bodies which I mentioned, the assembly of the municipality, the Executive Council, and the Crisis Staff, that they proposed to the Supreme Defence Council for the Republic of Croatia to propose to the United Nations to the European Union for a demilitarised zone to be established in the city of Dubrovnik with weapons being handed over to the international forces, or that everybody who is incapable of combat be evacuated from the area of Dubrovnik, and so on and so forth? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here: I cannot talk competently about some things here on a hearsay basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you ever heard about it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. I did hear about these things, but I'm telling you that I cannot speak about these things competently, because I was not officially informed by people who should have known about these things, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what did you hear about this particular thing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just said, that the city was to be evacuated and in this way preserved, because it was better to save the city than to remain there and have the people suffer and the city suffer consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the proposal about demilitarised zone set by the city of Dubrovnik to the supreme state council?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I repeat: I cannot speak about this competently because I was not officially informed about these things, nor did I seek any information on this via official channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The proposal coming from Dubrovnik for the demilitarisation to the supreme state council is something that you did not hear about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But privately you did?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, privately there was word about this. But as I said, I cannot competently speak about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was being said privately about this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what you said, that the city should be evacuated, that the people should leave the city to save it from bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear privately about the proposal coming from Dubrovnik for the city to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, apart from what I heard, apart from having heard that there was a proposal to that effect as well. But I did not get any such information from qualified people. But I repeat: Seeing where I was in the period under review, you can also conclude for yourself whether I was in a position to hear this from competent people and officially. If I was on the road all the time, and also in hospital during that month, I was in no position to receive such information in the way that you want me to tell it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you have supported at the time a proposal by the Executive Council, the Crisis Staff, and the mayor on demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You don't have to answer that question, Mr. Mustac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To this last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, don't answer it, Mr. Mustac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I should reply to it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from your private contacts what was the fate of this initiative that I just talked about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who dismissed this initiative?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was also -- this was the mayor himself, with his team. The mayor and his team also dismissed this initiative, and it was not brought up again after the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So do you know from private sources that the mayor dismissed his own initiative, basically?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. That is to say, I don't know about this initiative officially, meaning I was not directly informed, nor did I ask about it. At the time, I was absent from Dubrovnik most of the time. But after the accomplished fact, the 6th of December events, I know that this initiative which was being discussed in the corridors was dismissed, namely, that no one supported it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the position of the citizens of Dubrovnik was in regard of this initiative?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that many people protested against it, that in fact a concert, a concert was held in the open, in front of the church of St. Basel, St. Vlac [phoen]. But I wasn't there at the time, but I was told that in protest against such an initiative, this concert was held to protest such a solution which would ostensibly help preserve, save the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ever open fire from the walls, from the ramparts of the Old Town towards JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a citizen, as a deputy, I sincerely state here that I simply do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything said about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard a story, how some persons -- one man had opened fire from his rifle, to which I said that that was ridiculous and stupid for anyone to air one's human misery, one's distress, one's dejection, to express it in this way, because this led nowhere. That was on one hand. On the other hand, it was wholly ineffectual because it was stupid to open fire from a air rifle towards any target. And whether it was precisely from the ramparts, I really don't know. I have no information whatsoever. That is to say, I personally did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said someone fired from an air rifle. How do you know exactly what the weapon being used was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was under quotations marks. I was talking about laughable weapons, as I said. So that's how the air rifle came to mind. You could perhaps imagine that it was a hunting rifle or something like that, a rifle which did not exactly have a five-kilometre range.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would propose a break now, if this is a convenient time. I only have two or three questions left for this witness. Therefore, I think ten minutes will be enough to -- for me to conclude my cross-examination, after the break, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mustac, please tell me: From whom did you hear these stories about fire being opened on the JNA positions from the old ramparts?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear this from anyone, in the sense of your question. There was no fire being opened. I said it a hundred times. I said that there were from time to time some laughable people - that's what I heard - who used their own weapons to fire, to open fire. What they were aiming at, I didn't know. I said this a number of times, that I thought it was laughable. So that's my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Who did you hear this from, since you didn't personally witness this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How would you qualify those people who did that, if they did it from the ramparts?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they did it, yes. You said that quite correctly. That's precisely what I'm telling you. I would characterise that, being an historian and knowing what it means that a town is a UNESCO World Heritage site. So that would be my answer. The town was a UNESCO World Heritage site, and in that town, there was no army. Anyway, the UNESCO observers and European monitors were in town at the time, and I am sure that they could confirm what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will read out to you a paragraph from your statement, and you will then please tell me whether the statement is correct.
