Answer: "I heard stories from some people who fired from the town walls on the JNA positions at Zarkovica. I personally did not see anyone do anything like that."

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given this statement to look at only when I arrived here on the 20th of this month, and the first thing I said was that I didn't say that. It was probably a mistranslation. But I did say what I said now during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if those were no scoundrels, as you said, how would you characterise those people?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would characterise them as laughable and irresponsible. They were in a town that is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and they were using this location to express their rage or their helplessness. I didn't think that was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you concerned by the fact that in a town where there had been no military units up until 1991, Nojko Marinovic came around and organised military units. It used to be a demilitarised town and now suddenly you had a town where a unit of the National Guard Corps or the Croatian army was stationed. Did this bother you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dubrovnik is a UNESCO World Heritage site. It became a world heritage site in 1979. But I'm talking about the town as defined intra murus. That's within the old walls. Everything that remained outside the old city walls was not a world heritage site.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question, or should I repeat my question? Were you concerned by the fact that in a town where there had been no military units before 1991, suddenly a military unit was set up, led by Nojko Marinovic? Were you concerned by this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This didn't worry me. Quite the contrary; this meant that a defence was being set up, because the town had already come under attack. This was some form of precaution, a form of defence, something that made it possible for us to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you see any mortars mounted on small lorries being moved from one location to another within the town itself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any cannon or guns mounted on small lorries or vans moving through the town, firing on JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not personally see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see an APC inside the Old Town at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see an APC, but as far as I know, this APC was a tool of communication between one section of the town of Dubrovnik and the occupied suburb of Mokosica. This APC, as you call it, was used to transport bread and other necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me get this right. The suburb of Mokosica that was under occupation was being supplied with bread by an APC from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were carrying bread -- well, you say that it was an APC. Well, that's what I was told too. That was the only possible means of communication at the time, under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this APC passed the defence lines, passed the JNA lines, reached Mokosica, and then drove back to Dubrovnik. Am I right in assuming this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was communication between the two ends. Whether it was an APC or not, I can't be quite sure. I'm not stating either. That's what I've heard. If you want, I can tell you the whole story about how I came to know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't think that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mustac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Usher, can I ask that the Prosecution Exhibit P39, as well as Prosecution Exhibit P10, be shown to the witness. I'm sorry. That's a correction. P12.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Sir, today in cross-examination, you said that you heard mortar fired from the Imperijal fort on the 6th of December, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what people said. I heard that from other people. I did not personally witness this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Looking at the colour map to your left, can you see the Imperijal fort on that map? That's Prosecution Exhibit P39.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Can that be placed on the ELMO maybe?

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Sir, I draw your attention to the map on your right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. One second. I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the Imperijal fort on this map?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on this map. It's not on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Can he be shown -- it's Prosecution Exhibit P10. It's a different map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify the Imperijal fort on that map, Prosecution Exhibit P10?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It's on the other side of the main road, the coastal road. There's a hill there called Srdj. And this is the Imperijal fort that was built by the French.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Sir, would it be correct to say, then, that the Imperijal fort is Srdj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to fold that map in the area in which he's identified the Imperijal fort and place it on the ELMO so that we can all see.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Sir, using the pointer, can you point again to identify the Imperijal fort.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness has pointed to Srdj on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you first hear the sound of mortar fire? Thank you. I'll conclude my redirect. Thank you. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mustac, thank you very much. That concludes the evidence you are asked to give. You are now free to leave the Tribunal. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. And I thank the Chamber for its understanding in my need to be out of the courtroom because of scheduling matters. The next witness is General Andrew Pringle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I wonder if you'd be kind enough to take the affirmation. If you would read the affirmation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Pringle, I will, in the interests of time, try to go not too quickly, but quickly enough so that the Chamber has an idea of your background through your career. But first, would you give us, please, your complete name.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Andrew Robert Douglas Pringle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And General Pringle you remember born on 9 October 1946 in Avington, England?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you have retired from military service in 2001?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In what branch of the military, General, did you serve, and with what rank did you retire?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: I was commissioned into The Royal Green Jackets which is a British army infantry regiment, and I retired in the rank of major general.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your retirement, have you undertaken a different occupation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. Since leaving the army I have become a defence consultant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What type of consultancy, if you are in a position to tell us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: I assist small and medium-sized companies in -- and high tech companies in dealing with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, just looking at your military background, from 1964 until 1966, you studied and completed your studies at the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Between 1969 and 1971, you completed studies at the Royal Military College of Science, with a bachelor of science degree, honours, in applied sciences?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 1978 to 1979, the Army Command and Staff College?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is that, General?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: That was the army staff college at Campbell in Surrey, England.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 1990, the higher command and staff course, which -- could you describe what that type of course entails and for whom it is generally directed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. That was a course for -- at that stage, especially selected officers in the army who were deemed to be destined for the highest positions, and its focus was particularly on strategy and campaign planning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 1991, the Royal College of Defence Studies. Again, is that a particular course of study, and is it geared for -- toward any type of candidate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a course for UK nationals drawn from the three armed services, from the Ministry of Defence, and in some instances, from British industry and the diplomatic corps, where they all get together for a year and concentrate on top leadership and managerial issues with a defence bias.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at your -- breaking down, or breaking your military experience into command and staff, looking at your command experience, in your 35 years or so in the military, is it correct that you have commanded at every level from platoon to division?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct. I've commanded from platoon, which is about 30 men, through company, which is about 100 to 120 men, through battalion battle group, which is up to 1.500 men, to brigade, five and a half thousand, to division, about 12 or 15.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that this long command career culminated in 1997 and 1998 when you served as commander of the multinational division, which I believe was also known as SFOR NATO, is that correct, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the rank of major general?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. It was multinational division south-west, which was part of SFOR based in Bosnia. I was actually based in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Banja Luka is in what part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, under the Dayton agreements?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Banja Luka is in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In 1995, I see that the reference to sector south-west Bosnia. Are we referring again to the same area, Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, we're not. We're -- in 1995 I commanded UN sector south-west, part of UNPROFOR force. My headquarters was based in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, with what rank did you carry out that task?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: In the rank of brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: UNPROFOR, could you very briefly describe what UNPROFOR is and what your particular mandate was.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was the UN protection force, mandated to supply humanitarian assistance to the civilian population of -- in my instance, Bosnia, during the Bosnian war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you in any way affiliated with any party to the conflict? Perhaps more --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Affiliated. I was not affiliated to any party to the conflict. I was part of the United Nations force which was entirely separate from the three parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: If that's the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is. In other words, there was no affiliation with any warring party, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: No. There was a lot of dealings with, but there was no affiliation with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dealing with all parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Dealing predominantly with the Bosnian Croats and the Bosniaks, because we were based in the federation area of Bosnia. Very little contact with Republika Srpska, because at that stage Republika Srpska wouldn't have UNPROFOR based on its territory. The only dealings I had at that stage with the Bosnian Serbs was in relation to the element of the British force that was in the enclave of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you use the term "Bosniaks," are you able to perhaps clarify with what group you may be referring or to what group?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: The Bosniaks. By the term Bosniaks, I'm talking about the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at your staff positions, General Pringle, they have included assistant director for military operations in the United Kingdom's Ministry of Defence, 1988 through 1991. What was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Full colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 1996 to 1997, director of land warfare, Ministry of Defence. What was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in this capacity, you indicated you headed what might be referred to as the British army's "think-tank." Could you perhaps explain what that was and what duties were entailed in that function.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. It was predominantly a branch dealing with concepts and doctrine looking forwards, charged specifically with thinking through the implications design of what we then called British army 2015.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which means?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Which means the size and shape and equipment and doctrine that would be applicable to the British army when we arrived at 2015.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, then, development of doctrine and concepts was part and parcel of this task?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Development of concepts and doctrine was part of the responsibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Between 1998 and 2001, you were chief of staff, permanent joint headquarters in the United Kingdom and what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Major general.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what types of responsibilities were folded into this --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: I was the chief of staff director of operations to the chief of joint operations, a three-star admiral at that stage. I was responsible for the planning and preparation of the UK's joint operations worldwide, and for heading up the permanent joint headquarters, a contribution to what was known as the defence crisis management organisation, which in simple terms is the permanent joint headquarters in the Ministry of Defence working together at the strategic operational interface, which effectively was formulating operational policy, and it would then fall to the permanent joint headquarters and myself, as the chief of staff, director of operations, in particular, to turn that policy into a plan and execution. And we did that during my time, from as far afield as East Timor, Sierra Leone, Middle East, Iraq, Bosnia, Kosovo, Albania, wherever we were operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, when you refer to joint operations, could you perhaps explain a little bit about what that concept is or what the term means?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Joint operations from the UK perspective is the integration of maritime, the land, and the air component into one harmonised force, in order to achieve the best objective. In other words, it's the execution using army, navy, and air force.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, in the course of your preparing to come to give your testimony at the Tribunal, you have prepared a report which has been filed and distributed, which you have entitled "Aspects of Command." And I would ask, if I could, that this report and its materials which are footnoted therein be provided now to the parties. Now, what I will inform the Chamber of is that we have a complete set of the materials. If the Chamber wishes the full set for footnotes. Otherwise, we have taken the parts which are actually referred to, because it would be very voluminous. Should the Chamber need it, it is certainly available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's very hard to have a final view without any knowledge of the contents, Ms. Somers. But at the moment, that which is shorter has an attraction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I assure you that we will happily turn in the entire package for -- but it is voluminous. I am asked to just transmit to the witness, if the Chamber permits me, that the interpreters need to catch up. So if the general could monitor a little bit where the cursor is on the screen, it assists. I think it's a problem we always -- we take for granted here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, you -- the document which, and its supporting materials, which the Chamber and counsel have, was prepared along a line of tasking, is that correct, for this particular appearance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. I was posed a number of questions and asked to provide a document enunciating my view on the answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And does this document also include what we might call generic principles that would be applicable to any organised military, as opposed to just the JNA or just the British?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: I answered the questions predominantly generically and linked it, where appropriate, to the JNA. But in my view, I touch on command climate and what we've called two up/two down. They are generic aspects of command that would be applicable to any structured army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At this time I would seek to move into evidence these documents and be able to refer to them by the exhibit numbers, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You put that in the plural at that point, Ms. Somers. Are you indicating a document beyond that which is 03495248?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The "Aspects of Command" report is the document, and its supporting -- if it would be prudent to do it as a composite, we can do that. Otherwise -- however the Registry finds it more suitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They're distinct documents. I think they should each be separately identified as an exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report will be Prosecution Exhibit number P40. The document, "Mission Analysis" will be Prosecution Exhibit number P41. That is bearing ERN number 03466653. The document bearing ERN number 00136805, Federal Secretariat for National Defence regulations, will be Prosecution Exhibit number P42. And document bearing ERN number 00797125 will be Prosecution Exhibit number P43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have a further document, 02148126 in the B/C/S language, with a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That document will be Prosecution Exhibit number P44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Has the Chamber -- has the Chamber declared them admitted? I'm sorry. Thank you very much. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Pringle, you had indicated that there were, before we even refer to the report, you had asked that I communicate to the Chamber that there is a typographical error that all who read should be aware of. On page 9 of your report, there are some footnotes at the top, and it quotes, at footnote 4, I'm told that should be footnote 14, and where it says footnote 7, it should read 17. And footnote 16 bears a correction in the translation of a title, to read "Rules for Land Forces Corps Provisional 1990." Rules for Land Forces Corps, c-o-r-p-s, Provisional 1990. Dealing with two distinct aspects of the report, let us start first with a concept which you have referred to as two up/two down. Can you please tell us what you actually mean by it, understanding that, of course, we have the report to work from, but that to clarify it and orient us a bit more directly.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll refer to my report and amplify it, if that's useful. Every commander has to understand the part he has to play in the wider course of events. That's what we refer to as two up. That is to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to pause, please, General. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies for interrupting the witness and Ms. Somers. The document that has been marked as P44, the last two pages of the translated text, L006347, as far as I am able to see, these pages are completely unrelated to the document under discussion. Even the page numbering does not correspond. Therefore, this must be an oversight, I assume. I just wanted to bring this to the attention of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There appears to have been a compilation error, Ms. Somers. Could that be attended to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll examine it. But I'm told that -- if I can just --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The explanation is that it is a longer range, or a larger range for the document, and we have taken those relevant parts -- that the footnotes have referred to. The entire document would be significantly longer, and I will certainly check it again. My recollection was that it was just those portions referred to. If it is not -- if we were wrong, we'll clean it up. We apologise for any inconvenience. We thought we had it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. So at the moment you put it on the basis that these are relevant extracts?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic, we'll receive it on that basis for the moment, unless some correction is brought forward later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I am entirely certain that this was just an oversight, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm sorry, General. We did interrupt your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll start again. Two up and two down is the subject and the question, and it really refers to a generic thought process that all commanders would have to go through in exercising their command. Two up is shorthand for thinking two up, which is a requirement that a commander will have to go through in order to fully understand the part he has to play and his command has to play in achieving the objective in the wider aspect of what is required. So he has to think about what his higher commander is trying to achieve and what part he has to play in that. That's thinking two up. Two down is slightly different. This is a thought process that a commander would go through, particularly when allocating tasks, because he has to be satisfied that the task he is allocating to subordinates is within their capabilities and resources. And he would do that by a mental check process of thinking two down. Now, if I give of example of what I'm talking about: If a brigade commander, for example, is tasking two separate battalions, that's one down, but those two battalions are composed of different elements. Let's say one is a full-strength battalion that has not been committed so far and has full companies and all its constituent parts, and let's say the other battalion has been committed, has taken heavy casualties, only has two companies and has taken a bit of a hammering. Well, in allocating tasks to those two battalions, by thinking two down to company level, the commander will have in his mind it would be unreasonable to give the full-strength battalion -- or let's put it around the other way. It would be unreasonable to give the half-strength battalion the same sort of tasks that I'm giving the full-strength battalion, because they don't have the same resources. And so the task that he would give them would be tempered to their resources and capability. And he's gone through a mental check to come to that analysis by thinking two down. So that's what we mean by two up and two down. And in my view, that's generic to any commander in any army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Pringle, the example that you gave about understanding the reality of resource allocation, are you suggesting that the commander then must know, really, what is happening on the ground to know what can realistically be tasked? And if you are suggesting that, how does the commander keep abreast of or learn in the first instance of what's happening on the ground at these levels?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, yes, I am suggesting that. And every commander, if he is to exercise his command effectively, must have a very good understanding and knowledge of what all parts of his command are doing and what state they're in, from morale through to equipment, through to personnel states. Now, all armies will have a system of reporting such that different levels of command will report up the chain of command to a specific laid-down programme and format on specific issues. What is my personnel state, what is my ammunition state, what is my -- what significant logistic problems do I have, or whatever. And that would be passed up from headquarters to headquarters, with each headquarters receiving it, required to take the necessary action at their level. So commanders would, through that system of reporting, be appraised of what is happening. That is a sort of slightly more -- slightly formal process. There's then the constant radio communications and passage of reports, minute by minute, which a high-level commander won't necessarily be sitting there listening to a radio, but his headquarters, his staff who are exercising control in his name, will be assimilating all that and keeping the commander up to date and appraised, as required, of significant events. And last but not least, a commander will keep himself abreast of the state of his command, if I can put it like that, by visiting his units and troops and looking the commanders in the eye and talking to the soldiers and actually sniffing the battlefield, if I can put it like that, and that's a very important aspect where he can get his own view, his own personal view of what is happening, what the problems are, what the issues are, and add that or compare that with what he's being told by his staff. So all of that comes together in a way designed to ensure that the commander knows what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, when you talk about commanders visiting, or sniffing, as it were, are you referring to all levels of command, from the highest, let's say, general to whatever the lowest level of command would be?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. But how far forward you can visit rather depends on how high up the chain of command you are. A divisional commander would spend a lot of time talking to his brigade commanders, for example, and he might on occasion go forward and talk to the battalion commanding officers. But he would spend a lot of time talking to his brigade commanders. A commanding officer of a battalion would be in constant touch with his company commanders and would be -- would visit them a lot. And because a company is a much smaller element in a much smaller space, he would probably rub shoulders with the soldiers as well, constantly. So it rather depends on what level in the chain of command you are, how far forward you get. I mean, for a divisional commander to visit a front-line trench, which I have to say is something that most divisional commanders would constantly like to do, but there's not enough time, really, to go forward in that detail. What is really important is that he is -- he and his subordinate commander are absolutely at one mentally on what the issues are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And so if, let us say, the highest level was unable to physically visit the front, there should still be no qualitative difference in what he knows about what is happening on the front because of the doctrinal position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. Because when the divisional commander is, say, visiting his brigade commander, the brigade commander will be talking to him about what he has learned from his last visit forward to his battalions or companies. So the fact that the divisional commander is not actually been right forward to the forward trench himself does not mean that he's not aware of what is going on. All this reporting and visiting and looking people in the eye that I'm talking about is all designed to ensure that the commander is fully aware of what's going on right down to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So an army level or army-size level or corps-size level commander who may not visit the front line would, under doctrine, have the same information relayed up?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is why the system of reporting is laid down in doctrine, in order that the commander and his headquarters are kept fully informed of what they need to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So if going two down would be exceeding, perhaps, the level at the very lowest on the ground level, it would seem under your explanation to be irrelevant, that the explanation would nonetheless, through doctrine, be passed up?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the speakers kindly slow down and remember to pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you put your question again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So if going two down might exceed perhaps the level of the lowest level on the ground, the actual guy in the trenches, it would make no difference according to what you're saying because doctrine picks up where the actual physical two down might be exceeded?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, when I was talking about two down, I was talking about a mental process of thinking two down. You're putting the question in -- I think what you're saying is if a commander can't visit two down, or further down than that, does that mean that he cannot be aware of what's going on at those levels? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On those lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: If that's the question, the answer to that is: Of course he is aware of what's going on at those levels. Whether he is able to visit it or not. Because of the reporting mechanisms that we've just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a British army general, had you had an opportunity to do any investigation or research into how this particular concept finds its way, if it does specifically or by analogy, in JNA doctrine?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I had a look at JNA doctrine, and if I refer you to the two up/two down part of the report I wrote, on page 8, and it's footnote 17, and there, for example, is an extract that comes straight out of rules for land forces corps provisional, where it says: "The work of the corps command upon receipt of an assignment comprises...", amongst other things, "...studying and understanding the assignment. Understanding the assignment means grasping the objectives of the action; the superior commander's idea of manoeuvre; the place and role of the corps within the framework of an assignment for several units, and the resulting tasks of the corps..." Now, that's a mixture of two up and two down, if you like, but it's remarkably similar. It's remarkably similar to the extract I've quoted, which is straight out of a British army manual, which is at footnote 14, which puts the same sort of notion but in different words.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking now, perhaps, to the second aspect of your report, which you have called "command climate." I'd like to get a little bit of preliminary understanding before we deal in detail about your explanations. Are there similarities, General, between principles of command and control in the British army and most armies, including the JNA during the time of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: I would say the principles are very similar. Command and control is about commanders executing their command and their staff controlling, taking the controlling measures in order that the commander's wishes are executed. Now, the notions are described using different words in different armies, but the principles and the functions, when you look at them, are very similar. I mean, the execution of command, whether you are in the JNA or the British army or the French army or the American army, carries the same sort of constituent parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What principles, if you are able to distil them down, would you view as perhaps the most essential to the functioning of any army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I think the first sort of principle I would put my finger on is that -- is the role of the commander himself and the function he plays, and this sort of brings us into sort of command climate. Because any commander at any level, in any army, through dint of the authority invested in him as a commander, has a responsibility to give orders, execute his mission, and see it through to fruition. But it's more than that, because all commanders will do that, perhaps in different ways personally. And the way they command may differ considerably. Some may command predominantly from their headquarters, some may command from very far forward, some may command from very far in the rear. Depending on a whole host of things. But predominantly, personal style and also communications, because a commander has to place himself where he is best able to influence events. So if he's best able to influence his events at the nodal point of communications and intelligence, where he is best informed, then that's probably where he will spend a lot of his time. And I would, in that instance, quote, for example, I believe General Franks commanding the American forces in the Gulf did not leave Qatar from start to finish. That didn't mean he didn't know what was going on. He didn't leave Qatar as I understand because that's the best place for him to be to know exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Because that's where all the communications, intelligence, and information, that was the hub, if you like. If he divorced himself from that headquarters, then there might have been aspects of that totality of information that would have dropped away because the communications weren't there. Now, I'm just using that generically. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have in part. I have a bit more of an inquiry. Perhaps when you discuss the term "orders," are you able to tell us what the superior commander's obligation as to orders is and what the subordinate obligation is as to orders? How would you, in a few words, explain that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, a superior commander would, if he's right at the top of the chain of command, he will initiate the orders. If he's further down, he will receive orders, analyse those orders he has received, work out what he has to do, and then issue orders based on that to the constituent parts of his command. And that will go on right down the chain of command, with each level analysing what they have got to do at their level and giving orders to their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, will the subordinates have an obligation toward somehow informing about the results of actions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: The subordinates have an obligation, A, to carry out the order; and B, to do everything that is required to execute those orders properly and professionally, which includes keeping their commanders fully informed as to what they are doing so that the appropriate coordination measures or reactions or whatever is required can be taken. I mean, once you've received an order, you do not execute it in isolation, without telling anybody. The military objectives in general terms are achieved by the effective coordination of all the moving parts, in such a way that they are harmonised to best effect. Now, that requires an all-informed network, if I can put it like that, so that everybody knows what everybody else is doing. So that the commanders can make the right decisions on actions that need to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have used a phrase on page 7 of your report, where you say: "Some armies operate to methodical planning and detailed orders and tight control." Can you perhaps indicate why you said this? Is there a distinction to be made between philosophies of command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, in general terms, an army will either operate to that form of doctrine, which I think in German is described as Behweldtaktik or it will operate to what in English we describe as mission command, what was taken from German World War II experience really known as Auftragstaktik, which is a form of command where subordinates are expected to and have much more latitude to use their initiative, providing they truly understand the higher commander's intent. The former, more detailed orders type of doctrine really requires subordinates to carry out the orders they have been given, and once they have achieved that objective, they await new orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is there -- are there any sets of circumstances, perhaps in the staffing of armies, that would mandate or suggest the wisdom of relying on one philosophy over another?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: The Auftragstaktik, mission command type of philosophy requires a specific doctrine, detailed training, a fundamental understanding at all levels of what part everybody has to play, a culture where the use of initiative, and therefore, by implication, an acceptance of the occasional mistake, if you like, is all part and parcel of it. Now, that really means that -- that's more appropriate to a professional army, where the officers and soldiers are long-serving, where they are experienced, and where their knowledge base is quite extensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How does that come about, to have the extensive knowledge base? What would have to occur to have that set of conditions dominate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the knowledge base will come from the training they receive. The operations they conduct and the experience they gain, and the successive courses that they would receive through their career. So I didn't quite finish. Can I -- that's the -- your question was what type of doctrine suits what sort of army. And what I've said so far is that the sort of mission command, use of a lot of initiative, is more appropriate to a professional army with long-serving officers and soldiers and a lot of experience. The much more detailed form of Behweldtaktik doctrine is more appropriate to a conscript army, perhaps, where there is enormous through put, where soldiers are serving for a lesser time, albeit there may be a corps of regular officers and NCOs, but where the same detailed knowledge base and experience cannot be taken for granted because it doesn't exist. And therefore, the soldiers, in order to execute their orders, will need much more detailed orders and much more detailed supervision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And why would they need that? What would happen if the detail were not there, or the supervision were not there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, they probably wouldn't have the experience to be able to judge what they should do next or what they should do, or they may decide because they don't have the experience, decide to take a course of action which, had they had greater experience, they would not have chosen. And therefore, the onus lies on the commanders to execute a tighter form of command with constant supervision, direction, and redirection, as required.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Returning to the concept of command climate: What is it? I mean, is it some mysterious force that hovers over a commander? What really is it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, it's not rocket science, that's for sure. Command climate, I mean, is a term that the British have coined, and I think the Americans use it as well, to describe the climate that is created by a commander. Now, any commander in any army will create a climate. Genghis Khan and Attila the Hun had a certain command climate I would suggest in their force of marauders. Guderian or whoever, any general, creates a command climate. And from the moment he walks into his office on first appointment he is beginning to set that climate, and it reflects the way he is, the way he acts, what he says, what his views are, how he executes command, how he deals with problems. All of that goes to create a climate. What he does when something goes right, what he SDS when something goes wrong, what actions he takes. Does he take a blind eye to certain events or does he -- is he a rigorous disciplinarian? All of that encapsulates what we call the command climate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What types of factors would impact upon the, first of all, the creation of the climate, and then perhaps the alteration of the climate of command over time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Command is a very personal thing and all commanders command in their own personal way. And therefore, the key factor in creating a command climate is the personality of the commander himself. You know, some might be very authoritarian. Some might not tolerate the slightest mistake. Some might metaphorically have a reputation for shooting the messenger and bad news is just not acceptable. Now, the sort of climate that that sort of commander creates is one where, you know, if bad news is not acceptable, then you won't be told bad news. If he is a hectoring and bullying type of commander, he cannot expect a free discussion from his subordinates. He's much more likely to be told what they think he wants to hear. On the other hand, a commander at the other end of the spectrum, who is easy to communicate with, you know, congratulates good acts, is tolerant of mistakes, providing they don't occur twice and providing people learn from them, but doesn't jump down people's throats when they're required to use initiative just because they got it wrong, he makes sure that they realise why they got it wrong so that they can get it right next time, a guy that wants to be told -- he wants to be kept informed as to the realities of the situation without people thinking about whether this is going to be popular news or not. If that's the sort of climate he creates, then that's the sort of command he will execute and that's the sort of response he will get from those he's commanding. So it's a very personal thing and it comes -- it exudes directly from the commander and he starts exuding that from the -- from day one that he takes up command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You've made reference to a certain tolerance for mistakes made the first time. Now, by "mistakes," you are not saying, or are you, breaches of order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: No. Breaches of order is not a mistake. By mistakes, I'm talking about perhaps somebody taking a course of action with the best of intents, which, had he thought about it more deeply or taken other factors into account, he might have done it another way. That's a mistake. You know, we all learn from experience, and perhaps, you know, somebody who is, you know, of lesser experience, as we've all seen it, we've all done it ourselves, has done something which on reflection you might have done it another way had you known one or two or factors to put into the pot. But that's not breaches of orders. Breaches of orders are breaches of orders and that is serious to a commander because if a commander gives an order because he wants that order executed, that's not a basis for discussion. A breach of order in any army is serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If a commander gives an order or passes on an order, now, you've said which he wants executed, what if he doesn't really want it executed but he has to pass it on? How does command climate perhaps come into the picture there, where in the chain an order is passed on, and yet there is perhaps less than enthusiasm about the content of the order? Where does climate come into play there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I think we come back to the personality of the commander. I mean, if a commander is passing on an order with which he has reservations, then before he passes that on, he will have discussed that with his superior, who has given him that order, which he has a duty to do. Because he may have been given an order which doesn't actually take all factors into account, and therefore, the commander, when he goes back to his superior who has given him the order and they discuss that, his superior will either say: Yup, I'm aware of that, but I've decided to do it this way regardless. Or he will say: That's a good point. Thank you for that. Well, let's amend that and let's do it this way. But there comes a point when a decision is made and when that decision is made, that order is the order. Now, the commander faced, if we've reached that point, if he's now faced with executing an order with which he is still unhappy, now we come straight to command climate, back to command climate and the personality of the commander. A wise commander would now realise that it is his duty to execute that command, and he would give orders and supervise its execution as if it was his own order. An unwise commander will give the order with a lot of back-chat and asides about I don't really like this, I think this is a stupid order, I disagree with this, I don't know why we've been told to do this. He's going to be unwise because he will find that his subordinates will be left confused. They will be left confused as to whether they're really meant to carry out this order or not. And his command will begin to fracture, and his authority will suffer as a result.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you saying, General, then, that mixed signals have a negative impact upon the command climate and upon command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Mixed signals will affect the execution of command considerably. Mixed signals will come from a certain sort of -- could come from a certain sort of command climate. You know, in generic terms, you know, maybe this is a, you know, rather let's say generically self-satisfied and rather disloyal command climate, where the commander is only happy to pass on things that he's in absolute agreement with, but if he doesn't like what he's being told to do by his superior then he thinks there's latitude to be disloyal and disagree and do it another way or not do at all. That sort of command climate will create complete confusion down the chain of command. And that sort of commander should not be surprised if his orders aren't carried out. Or if somebody decides to carry out an order in another way, assuming that that's really what the commander wants him to do, even though he hasn't actually said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What would your view be as to the impact on the obligation to discipline and the disciplinary process where command -- where orders are transmitted in such a way where there are either mixed signals or perhaps some form of connivance or perhaps some nuance that suggests that the order is not really a problem if it's not carried out? What happens to the entire process?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, under those circumstances, what you begin to get is the commander begins to lose authority. Those he is commanding begin to get extremely confused about what's a real order and what isn't. If he's -- if orders are being passed caveated with they don't really matter, and then other things are done instead which might be contrary to discipline and other orders and no action is taken, all of that begins to create a command climate where, you know, we're heading for a command climate of anarchy and anything goes under those circumstances. This is not a concept of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, just returning for one minute to your distinction between -- I guess you'd call them centralised, order detailed, order-driven armies and mission-command armies. Based on your understanding from experience and perhaps from further investigation as to the JNA of the period of this indictment, let's say 1991, in which camp would you be more likely to place the JNA: The initiative-driven or the more detailed order-driven?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: From my reading of their doctrine and from limited experience, I would put them in the orders-driven camp rather than the mission-command camp. And that's not a derogatory comment in any way. That would simply reflect their requirements. I mean, they were a conscript army. At this stage we're talking about a conscript army, albeit with a regular corps of extremely well-trained officers and NCOs, but a huge number of recently mobilised conscripts and territorial-force soldiers and officers, without the same standard of training and knowledge and experience as their regular counterparts in the JNA. And therefore, as I said earlier, whatever army you're in, if that's the raw material you have to play with, then you're going to have to have a very tight command and control system and very tight supervision in order to make sure that your orders are being carried out in the way you want them and in a militarily sensible way. I mean, it was General Patton who once said that giving the orders is the easy part. Actually seeing that it happens is the difficult part. So that's not unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, you referred a few moments ago to what could happen if orders which are passed, and let's say this is an active process, a recently passed order, is either not implemented or is breached, and the effect of perhaps absence of discipline on that process. I'd ask you now about orders that are standing orders, an order is in place for a period of time and is transmitted through doctrine to all persons. What would your view be of a command in which a violation of the order occurs, with no inquiry, no -- call it investigation, no reaction from command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: My immediate reaction would be that command is broken down, for whatever reason; that the authority of the commander is undermined, for whatever reason. I mean, if there is standing operational instructions on whatever subject that are being flagrantly disobeyed, then all those in the chain of command have a responsibility to do something about it. And if they fail to do something about it, their superior has a responsibility to do something about the original transgression of orders and the failure of the immediate superior commander to fail to do something about it. So if you're postulating what is the effect on command if orders are given, disobeyed, and nothing happens about it, the real effect of that is that it will begin to create a view at grass roots level that some orders seem to matter and others don't, and these ones which are flagrantly transgressed and nobody does anything about it must therefore be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, what you're suggesting is that it becomes someone who is receiving the order who decides whether an order should be obeyed or not. Is that my understanding of what you just said?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Under those circumstances that you just described, if some are adhered to and implemented but some are not, then where is the -- does discretion figure in?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: There is no discretion in the carrying out of orders, unless -- well, I'm talking very generically. Let's try and be a bit more specific. Let's say that the rules of armed conflict require that prisoners will be treated humanely and prisoners will, for example, not be shot. But the commander is slightly concerned that the blood is up and, you know, some of his more hot-blooded subordinates may take a different view. Now, he would immediately, if he was concerned about that, impress on his chain of command. Now, watch this: "We've taken a hammering. The blood is up. It's under these sort of circumstances where there can be a breakdown of discipline and bad things can happen. Now, impress on all your commanders to the lowest level that this is not to happen." Now, if it then does happen and nothing is done about it, well, then those that perpetrated the crime will begin to think that: Well, they're only telling us these orders because they think they have to, because it's, you know, that's what doctrine says. But actually the way we're going about business now is shooting prisoners and that seems to be acceptable, and the next time we catch prisoners, we'll shoot them too. I'm using that as a generic answer rather than just talk in very general terms. So if there is a specific order which is disobeyed and nothing is done about it, that creates the impression at all levels that that order is not serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, I'm sorry to intrude, but is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Before we proceed, may I offer to the Chamber, through the Registry, the corrected pages in translation. Our sincerest apologies. It apparently was a printing -- literally off-the-printer error, and we do apologise for any inconvenience to all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Pringle, just to help you refresh where we left off, we were discussing the example of -- I think you called it hot-bloodedness and what might happen if there were no anticipated action by a commander, and in fact, the concern over which the commander -- or which the commander had materialised. Can I ask you if I've understood correctly that a commander has a duty to anticipate the various types of reactions, problems, possibilities of distress that might arise in his subordinates? Is this part of his duty and is it reflected in the command climate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. A commander is expected to know his command. He's meant to know the strong points, the weak points. He's meant to know where problems might appear and where problems won't appear. He will know who he can rely on absolutely ultimately, and he'll know who he has to pay rather more attention to. He will know who has to be kicked on, in a equestrian terms, and he will know who has to be reined in, in equestrian terms. Now, your question was about anticipation. So in giving an order, all these things will be in his mind, and having given the order, and we return to General Patton, making it happen is the difficult part, he would then take whatever actions he thought necessary to ensure that that order was properly understood and was properly executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How much does a commander have to know about his subordinates? And when I say subordinates, not just in the chain of command, but about those who are commanded by those in the chain of command, the troops. How much does he have to know about problems, issues, and how would he learn that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: I think I'd answer that, in the first instance, by differentiating between levels of command. I mean, a company commander with 100, 120 men, providing they've been together for a certain amount of time, will know all those men. He might even know their wives and children's names in some instances. He will have spent a lot of time with them and he will know them, and he will have a detailed knowledge of who are the really reliable ones, who are the less reliable ones, who needs close supervision, who can be relied upon to use their initiative. And that's relatively easy at that level. Now, as you go up the chain of command, you can't -- you obviously cannot have that intimate a knowledge down to that level. But what is important is that at whatever level you are, you know your subordinate commanders extremely well and you probably know quite a lot about their subordinate commanders. So that's two levels down. It may be that, through conversation between commanders, a commander will become aware that there is a particular problem person in one element of a command, fairly low level down. So his attention will have been drawn to it, which he then, depending on how seriously he views that, may concentrate on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, then, that it's driven more by circumstances -- that the principle remains in place, that one way or another, the commander will know what's going on down there, maybe not on a "intimate" level?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: He will -- yes. That's a slightly different issue. He will know what's going on because of all the reporting mechanisms that we've previously discussed. I've answered your previous question rather in terms of knowing the personalities involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If disciplinary issues arise as a result, perhaps, of personality -- of personalities, is this a matter that through doctrine or reporting would come to the attention of the commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. And in most armies, including the JNA, the duties of the commander are laid down in doctrine in respect to breaches of discipline. And in short order, if there is a serious breach of discipline, or a breach of discipline, the immediate commander has a duty to deal with it if he's empowered to deal with it, or refer it to the next level up if he's not empowered to deal with it. The receiving level of command then has the responsibility to deal with it if they are empowered to deal with it, but refer it to the next level up if they are not empowered to deal with it. And so on. So a serious breach of discipline will be passed up the chain of command in accordance with the standing operational procedures in place and in accordance with the doctrine laid down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A serious breach of discipline may or may not involve criminal behaviour; is that correct? Can it be violation or breach of an order?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, breaches of discipline will come in all shapes and forms, and if a soldier fails to salute his officer, that is a local level breach, minor, petty breach of discipline that can be dealt with at local level. If, on the other hand, a breach of discipline entails something, you know, truly serious, like a breach of international law, or a breach of the Geneva Conventions, then that is a serious breach of discipline that would have to be referred up to the appropriate level of command that is empowered to deal with that. And since that is a criminal matter, that would be, you know, the top level of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You just alluded to breaches of conventions, and I wanted to ask you about the obligation of a commander to ensure that his subordinates know and understand their obligations with regard to the laws of conflict or any term you wish to use, but laws of war, laws of conflict, international humanitarian law, the principles that govern conduct on the battlefield. How is that accomplished?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's accomplished through training. Part of the preparing of formations, units for operations involves the training of them in all aspects that they need to be aware of. And that's not just tactical aspects and the use of weapons and coordinating fire support and all of that; it also includes awareness training of the duties of every individual in terms of the laws of armed conflict that that state has signed up to or are internationally appropriate. And in general terms, we're talking about the laws of armed conflict which fall from the Geneva Convention. And in general terms, every soldier should be briefed on the circumstances which he's likely to find himself in when, for example, he takes a prisoner, or when, for example, he finds himself coming into contact with the civilian population, or when, for example, he comes across an enemy wounded soldier. The way he's expected to conduct himself is laid down in international law, and more importantly, what he is not expected to do is also implied there. Now, part of preparation for combat will be training in all those aspects, assuming, of course, one has the time to do that. If you don't have the time to do that, and you have an army that is not experienced, then there is an additional onus on the commander, because now he's faced with the prospect where things could go wrong in this respect, and he has an additional responsibility to take whatever measures he deems necessary to ensure that these potential pitfalls are overcome. And if you like, he would -- this would be on-the-job training and briefing and drawing this to the attention of his subordinate commanders, saying, you know: "I'm worried about these aspects. We've received a large number of new recruits. Perhaps they haven't been fully trained. I don't believe they've been exposed to the laws of armed conflict. Make sure that they are briefed on how to conduct themselves when, for example, they come across wounded soldiers, they come across civilians, they come -- they take prisoners. And make sure that they understand and, in particular, make sure that the chain of command, the non-commissioned officers and the officers, in particular, make sure that they understand and make sure that they impress that on their soldiers." There's an added, additional onus on the commanders, the less experienced, the less well trained the soldiers are.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The obligations that you have referred to in the conventions, and I would submit the protocols as well, would you view that a commander would have an obligation to be sure that his subordinates knew not only about the civilian population but perhaps about sensitive sites or other categories enumerated in those documents you referred to? Let's say even special, cultural, or what -- that type, religious, particularly if indigenous to an area.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. A commander -- a high-level commander will be fully aware of the doctrine and the rules and regulations under which his army operates. He will also be aware, if they are now entering war or a combat situation, that some of these things are very rapidly going to pass from theory and classroom teaching to reality. And he will also be aware of the situation in which his troops are likely to find themselves and will concentrate, I would suggest, in priority on the specific aspects that are pertinent to that area of operations. Now, in committing his soldiers to combat, they are all going to need to know about dealing with prisoners of war. They are all going to need to know about dealing with civilians. They are all going to need to know about what actions to take when they come across a wounded enemy. If he is operating in an area where the constraints surrounding cultural heritage sites also enter into his bailiwick, knowing that that is in his doctrinal pamphlet, the application of international laws of war and the armed forces of the SFRY, he will also, or should, I suggest, also take action to impress down the chain of command that in this particular instance, make sure that your actions are conversant with this law, our doctrine, our policy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I note that you made reference to what is marked as Prosecution Exhibit 42. Are there -- are you able, very briefly, to just direct us to some of the provisions or sections which may deal with the matters you've just discussed that are required to be passed on by a commander to his subordinates, or at least required to be learned by those subordinates? In the interests of time, if I can turn your attention, perhaps, to page 35.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, this is a very detailed document, and the detail of this document, you can get a flavour from from the contents on page 3. And it includes everything, from violation of international laws of war, means and methods of combat, general restrictions and prohibitions, the wounded and the sick, prisoners of war. And that page that you have highlighted, page 35, actually deals with the concept of cultural property. Cultural property should be understood to mean ... And there it goes down. The provisions -- and that comes after prisoners of war and interment camps. So how soldiers are expected to act and react and what care they're meant to take in certain circumstances is all laid down in this SFRY document, as is -- and if I could refer you to page 15, paragraph 21: The responsibility for the actions of subordinates. And I think probably that's worth just reading. "An officer shall be personally liable for violation of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that units subordinate to him or other units or individuals were planning the commission of such violations and at a time when it was still possible to prevent their commission, failed to take measures to prevent such violations. That officer shall also be held personally liable who, aware that violations of the laws of war have been committed, fails to institute disciplinary or criminal proceedings against the offender, or if the instituting of proceedings does not fall within his jurisdiction, fails to report the violation of [sic] his superior officer."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Could you read perhaps a bit further? It doesn't end there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "An officer shall be answerable as an accomplice or instigator if, by failure to take action against his subordinates who violates the laws of war, he contributes to the repeated commission of such acts by units or individuals subordinated to him." So when I read this document, I mean, my overall impression was, you know, that's a brilliant document. That is a document that lays down exactly how any army should act, which is not surprising, because it's based on all the treaties that the various nations have signed up to. And the fact that it had been taken into the doctrine of the JNA I viewed as highly pertinent.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The role of enforcing discipline. Is discipline a significant factor in maintaining a favourable command climate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: When we talk about a favourable command climate, I think we're talking about a climate of command where the expectation that the right things will be done at the right time, to the right standards, and that disciplinary action will be taken as appropriate and when necessary, when breaches of discipline occur, that is, in a nutshell, what I think you would be referring to as a favourable command climate. If, therefore, when breaches of discipline occur, there is a failure to take the necessary action, then that will start to impinge on the authority of the commander and the climate, in that if it becomes common knowledge or accepted practice that, although, in theory, some acts are debarred, if I can put it like that, but when those orders are transgressed, nothing happens and no disciplinary action is taken, then there will be a growing assumption amongst the troops that those actions are acceptable, and therefore, the command climate that is now being created is one where a blind eye will be turned when certain actions are taken which have now become, in theory, laid down in doctrine, and orders, but not in actuality practiced or put into effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that they may be something like window dressing? Is that a term that would be appropriate to view that type of order that exists but is not adhered to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: I think that would be quite a suitable description of an order that is given but nobody cares less whether it's carried out or not. You know, window dressing, wallpaper. You can use whatever description you like, really, but it's not an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You are suggesting, then, just so I'm sure I understand you, that the evidence that no one cares if it's carried out or not is the absence of disciplinary undertakings in the event of the breach? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. When a breach of discipline occurs, and certain actions are laid down as necessary to follow up and deal with that breach of discipline, if those actions do not occur, then it will very quickly become common knowledge and accepted modus operandi that whatever the breach of discipline concerns is in fact accepted practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, you have just gone through the regulations of the SFRY, which you described as the binding regulations on the troops. And my question is: Is the fact that an obligation is indicated in that document sufficient to bind the lowest soldier?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. But unless he is trained accordingly, he may not -- the lowest soldier may not even know about it, and therefore, there is an onus on his commander to make sure that he receives the right training and awareness training so he understands that there is an onus on him. The fact that, you know -- I believe it's no defence in law when I shoot a prisoner to say: Well, I really didn't know that that was a breach of discipline. There is an onus on the commander to make sure that the soldiers know what their responsibilities are, and that is part of the responsibility of the commanders in training their troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a follow-up to your response: In a conscript army, or a rapidly mobilised army, would you view any need for a commander, or any requirement - let us make it a duty of a commander - to reinforce by supplementary order that which is contained in volumes that may or may not have made their way to the individual knowledge of every soldier?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I think we have to acknowledge that there's a practical problem. I mean, let's try and put ourselves into the mind of. We have fairly rapidly gone to war. We have rapidly mobilised. We've got a lot of -- some very well-trained soldiers and officers, some not very well-trained soldiers and officers, some hardly trained at all, and some irregulars; a mixed bag. But we're now entering war. War is a very serious issue. War is about killing people. And war is subject to a number of rules and regulations in its conduct. I would suggest that any responsible commander, under those circumstances, would realise that he had a serious responsibility to ensure that his soldiers, whatever their state of training, were now trained or alerted to those issues that the commander regarded as particularly important, and in particular, those issues which he regarded, because of the state of training, as most likely to go wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You just said issues that a commander views as particularly important. There seems to be some subjectivity in there. If, objectively, the law says that an issue is important - protection of an area, a sensitive area, a protected area - and that is deemed important at law, does the commander's subjective opinion of its importance have any real bearing on his obligation to make sure his troops are trained?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
