utterances.text: No. What I was -- the picture I was trying to paint was not the fact that the commander can pick and choose what orders he deems important and which he doesn't. What I was trying to paint was a picture of a rapidly mobilised army made up of a large amount of people of varying degrees of training. The fact of life that they were never going to be as well trained as he would have liked them in the perfect world, and he had to -- he has to compare the issues at hand and the requirements at hand with the scenario in which he is operating. And therefore, I think he would be asking himself: Now, what are the most likely -- what are the most -- I cannot train every soldier in all the details of this document now. You know, that would be the subject of extensive training over extensive courses, reinforced regularly so that it becomes second nature. That's not the circumstances we're in. But, he would say, in the circumstances that I now find myself in, the most likely things that my soldiers are likely to face are ... And I've enumerated some. And if he's operating in an area which includes a cultural heritage site, how to treat it quoted in that pamphlet, then he would be alert to that and he would say: And by the way, you know, in this specific area of operations, there are one, two, three, seven cultural sites that we must not harm in any way, and they are A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. So please mark them all on your map and be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Pringle, does the existence of an unfavourable command climate, for whatever reason, does the existence of such a climate negate or abrogate the command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: No. The commander's responsibility stems from his authority as the commander. The command climate is the climate he creates by the way he carries out his command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask, please, if the usher could assist us in distributing an exhibit of the Prosecution. The Prosecution has just presented a document which, in its English -- well, actually, the date of it is 29 September 1991, from the SSNO, the General Staff, military secret, highly confidential, purporting to bear a signature, or at least an endorsement by Chief of General Staff of the SFRY, Lieutenant General Blagoje Adzic. And it is addressed to commands of the 1st, 2nd, 5th VO, or Military District; VPO, Military Naval District; and RV and PVO, Air Force and Air Defence; OG-2, 2nd Operational Group; 5th Corps and 9th Corps. I hope I've read the "K" correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I'd ask you to turn your attention to paragraph 1, which indicates that -- which orders that: "Commands of VO and RV and PVO are to submit regular combat reports. Reports are to be submitted on the basis of the regular combat reports of the brigades and the corps, from three levels down (brigade-regiment, independent battalion-division) for all units and detached formations." Now, I am not suggesting for one minute that we are linking this to the other numbered concept of two up/two down. I'm moving away from that. But I'm asking you: What does this tell you about the information passage within the units that are addressed by General Adzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, the first line plainly indicates that there is concern and they are seeking a more efficient command and control and the execution of combat tasks. And I would glean from this that there has been concern about the detail and level of reporting going on, such that instructions are now being given to submit regular combat reports, and they're actually told in what detail to submit them, to three levels down. They're then instructed to submit these regular combat reports in line with the attached, I assume, doctrinal instructions, and then reminded that, in addition to regular combat reports, extraordinary reports on matters of importance should be passed up the chain of command without waiting, with an immediacy. There's then a reminder that regular combat reports are to be submitted by 2100 hours each day, to include the situation up to 1900 hours that day. This is all about information flowing up the chain of command, such that those at the highest levels of command are completely conversant as to what the issues are that might need their attention, and it is specifying in some detail the level down to which they should be reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General, if in fact there were a concern about information flow, and perhaps a problem, an issue arose, would that problem or concern on information flow absolve or abrogate the responsibility of the commander for what took place in his area of responsibility, or AOR?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: No. I think it's important perhaps to reflect on the fact that the commander is responsible for everything that happens in his command, everything: the conduct of his troops, their state of training, the way they execute tasks, the efficiency of his command, the passage of orders. All of that is the commander's responsibility. If the commander becomes aware that information is not flowing up the chain of command in the level of detail or with the immediacy that he would wish it, then he has a duty, probably executed through his staff, to correct that. If the commander -- well, if sufficient information is not flowing up the chain of command, or if certain information is deliberately being hidden from the higher levels of the chain of command, that is the commander's responsibility. That is his fault. That reflects the way he has executed his command. One of the joys of command is that you're responsible for everything. To him the credit, him the blame.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would at this time ask to admit into evidence the exhibit that has just been presented and discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be Prosecution Exhibit number P45.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: General Pringle, I would like to ask you a little bit about command climate and how it may be influenced or how its erosion, or in reinforcement, influences the conduct of soldiers on the ground. Let's say at the front. You've alluded to it. You've given examples of the shooting of a civilian or of a prisoner. But can you give examples where the climate has a direct and immediate impact on what happens on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the overall command climate, if I can put it like that, stemming from the top to the bottom, let's imagine that is made up of lots of constituent command climates, because every commander, as I said earlier, exudes a command climate of his own. It reflects the manner in which he conducts his command. So the way the soldiers conduct themselves will reflect the way they are commanded and the manner in which they are commanded by their superiors. So whatever doctrine and law says, the soldiers will actually take their lead from their commanders. They will very rapidly understand what is acceptable to their commanders and what is not, irrespective of what, if you like, doctrine and law has espoused as the laid-down way of doing things. So let's take some trivial examples. And I don't have a fetish about saluting, but let's take that. It has become acceptable in unit A that the soldiers call the officers by their Christian names and there are no compliments paid between ranks. Now, that would be against accepted code and conduct and it would begin to reflect on the way that unit is being run. But if that is the climate which is evolved, well, that's the way the soldiers will conduct themselves. If -- let's take a more serious example. If I belong to a certain unit which prides itself in its aggressive and courageous exploits but where prisoners are never taken and nothing is said about that, well, that will become the way that unit conducts itself, because that's the atmosphere, the climate of command that has grown up there. So at all levels, the climate of command reflects the manner in which the commanders execute their responsibilities, and it also reflects the manner in which their superiors take a view on the way those subordinates are executing their responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Accepting the premise that in hostilities, emotions may run high, what, nonetheless, could be the effect of the use or the encouragement of the use of terminology with regard to the other side, of course, call it the enemy, but the other side, what message is sent down when, from up on high, certain types of expression, phraseology is used in official communication? I could perhaps ask you to refine it more. Is there an element of dehumanisation that is at all encouraged in such a process?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I said when we started this discussion that a commander begins to create his own climate from the moment he first arrives, through his every action. All eyes, always, are on the commander. What the commander thinks, what the commander says, what the commander's views are, what the commander thinks is serious, what he thinks is not serious, how he conducts himself, all begins to create that climate. Now, if, hypothetically speaking, a commander referred to enemy forces in a particularly derogatory way that might indicate that they were really worthless and not worth worrying about, well, that message will be picked up down the chain of command and that commander should expect his subordinates' actions to reflect what they -- the message they are receiving from their superior commander, in the climate that he is setting. I mean, you'll remember that -- and I think the Americans in Vietnam were sometimes belaboured for, you know, referring to all the Vietnamese as -- whatever they referred to them as, gooks or something like that. Now, that started to create a climate where Vietnamese just didn't matter, and not an inconsiderable number of dreadful things happened, perhaps in part as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dreadful things would include, perhaps, violations of laws of war, international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. And the one I had in mind when I was thinking about that straight off the top of my head was the My Lai massacre. That sort of action cannot happen if people have been brought up, (a), to comply with the international laws of war; and (b), to have a respect for humanity, even if it is enemy humanity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Accepting that strategic decisions are not necessarily made on the battlefield or perhaps not embellished upon on the battlefield, what is your view of the command obligation to carry out a strategic order from above that may change in some way the initial plan for an operation? Example: Proceeding to a territory for certain objectives, change of plan is signaled from above, ceasefire to come into effect, no further operations. If unpopular with the commander, what is his obligation with regard to that order from above?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Whether that order or above is popular with a commander is irrelevant. He has a duty now to carry that out. If that is the orders he is being given, to move in this instance to a ceasefire, which may very well require amendment to orders already given, because orders already given were based on some other objective, like seize area alpha. The fact that we're now moving to a ceasefire would put a considerable onus on the commander to reflect on what changes in mission there now was and what actions his subordinate commanders were required to carry out in order to effect this change in direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how would the change in direction be communicated by the commander?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: He would communicate that in a variety of ways: Written orders, radio communications, data communications. Probably in this respect, a commander would deem there was a responsibility on him now to get round and visit his subordinate commanders and make sure they absolutely understood what the change in direction was, why it was coming about, and what part they had to play in it. So in this event, you could -- all channels of communication now would go to red hot. Change in mission, stop doing this, start preparing for that, implications for you are this, disengage, do not take any actions that might throw the ceasefire off course, do not be antagonised by the enemy. Hold firm where you are. Mission now is to bring this ceasefire into effect properly, without creating any conditions or the excuse that we threw it off course deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If in fact there is a disagreement or unhappiness by a commander in implementing the order, particularly from the strategic level, what would be the recourse of that commander before implementing, if there was such disagreement?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW ROBERT DOUGLAS PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I return to an answer to a similar question. If the high-level commander has received an order from a strategic sort of Ministry of Defence Belgrade type level, or whatever level, his higher level anyway, which he has really severe reservations about, then he has the right, indeed he probably has the responsibility, to return to, either physically or in communication terms, high level, and make his concerns known so that they are understood, whereupon he will either be told to -- the reason for it and to get on with it regardless, or his views will be taken into account. But once he is told: This is what we're now getting on with. Execute. Whatever his private view is, he has a responsibility to execute it, in exactly the same way that his subordinates have a responsibility to execute the orders he gives them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would anticipate the need for a bit of time tomorrow morning, not a lot. And if this would be an acceptable time to break, I will tailor my examination and trim it so that counsel opposite would have an opportunity to complete its examination and cross tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn, then, a few minutes early, and we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00. I must ask you to return, then, if you would. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
